subject: Biology
title: Biomolecules (Biology)
summary: Chemical analysis of living tissue gives an acid-soluble pool (micromolecules, molecular weight below ~1000 Da) and an acid-insoluble fraction (macromolecules — proteins, nucleic acids, polysaccharides; lipids appear here because membranes break into vesicles).
Proteins are polymers of amino acids (heteropolymers); polysaccharides are polymers of sugars; nucleic acids are polymers of nucleotides.
Enzymes are mostly proteins that speed up reactions by lowering activation energy. Their activity depends on temperature, pH and substrate concentration, and can be inhibited.
Enzymes are classified into six classes, and many need cofactors: prosthetic groups, coenzymes or metal ions.

formulas.name: Most abundant
formulas.formula: most abundant chemical in living organisms: water (70–90%);  most abundant protein in the animal world: collagen;  in the whole biosphere: RuBisCO

formulas.name: Amino acid
formulas.formula: α-carbon bonded to H, –NH₂, –COOH and an R group;  20 types;  zwitterion form at isoelectric pH

formulas.name: Lipids
formulas.formula: fatty acid + glycerol → mono-, di-, triglycerides;  saturated (no C=C) or unsaturated (one or more C=C);  phospholipids (lecithin) in membranes
formulas.note: Palmitic acid has 16 carbons (including the carboxyl carbon); arachidonic acid has 20.

formulas.name: Nucleotide
formulas.formula: nitrogen base + pentose sugar (nucleoside) + phosphate;  adenine, guanine (purines);  cytosine, uracil, thymine (pyrimidines)

formulas.name: Base → nucleoside → nucleotide names
formulas.formula: adenine (base) → adenosine (nucleoside = base + sugar) → adenylic acid (nucleotide = nucleoside + phosphate);  guanine → guanosine → guanylic acid;  cytosine → cytidine → cytidylic acid;  uracil → uridine → uridylic acid;  thymine → thymidine → thymidylic acid
formulas.note: Don't confuse adenine/adenosine with alanine — alanine is an amino acid (like glycine and serine).

formulas.name: Protein structure levels
formulas.formula: primary (sequence; N-terminal to C-terminal);  secondary (α-helix — right-handed);  tertiary (3-D folding);  quaternary (subunits — haemoglobin: 2α + 2β)

formulas.name: Bonds in polymers
formulas.formula: peptide bond (amino acids);  glycosidic bond (monosaccharides);  phosphodiester bond (nucleotides);  ester bond (fatty acid + glycerol)

formulas.name: Polysaccharides
formulas.formula: starch (helical, holds I₂ → blue);  cellulose (no complex helix, doesn't hold I₂);  glycogen (animal storage);  inulin (fructose polymer);  chitin (complex polysaccharide in exoskeletons and fungal walls)

formulas.name: Enzyme classes
formulas.formula: 1 oxidoreductases/dehydrogenases;  2 transferases;  3 hydrolases;  4 lyases;  5 isomerases;  6 ligases

formulas.name: Enzyme class reactions
formulas.formula: oxidoreductases: S reduced + S′ oxidised → S oxidised + S′ reduced;  transferases: S–G + S′ → S + S′–G (G = a group other than hydrogen);  hydrolases: break ester, ether, peptide, glycosidic, C–C, C–halide or P–N bonds by adding water;  lyases: remove groups without hydrolysis, leaving a double bond (X–C–C–Y → X–Y + C=C);  isomerases: interconvert optical, geometric or positional isomers;  ligases: join two compounds (C–O, C–S, C–N, P–O bonds)
formulas.when: Naming the class from a given reaction.

formulas.name: Michaelis constant and inhibition
formulas.formula: Km = substrate concentration at ½Vmax;  competitive inhibitor resembles substrate — malonate inhibits succinic dehydrogenase
formulas.note: A competitive inhibitor raises Km but Vmax stays the same.

formulas.name: Cofactors
formulas.formula: prosthetic group (tightly bound — haem in peroxidase, catalase);  coenzyme (loosely bound, often vitamin-derived — NAD, NADP from niacin);  metal ion (Zn²⁺ for carboxypeptidase)

formulas.name: Fastest enzyme
formulas.formula: carbonic anhydrase: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃, about 600,000 reactions per second (≈ 10⁷ times faster than uncatalysed)

formulas.name: Effect of temperature and pH
formulas.formula: activity rises to an optimum, then falls; low temperature inactivates reversibly, high temperature denatures

examples.title: Lipids in the acid-insoluble fraction
examples.problem: Lipids have small molecular weights, so why do they appear in the acid-insoluble pool?
examples.solution: When tissue is ground, cell membranes break into vesicles that are insoluble in acid, so the lipids come down with the macromolecules.

examples.title: Enzyme class
examples.problem: An enzyme removes groups from a substrate without hydrolysis, leaving a double bond. Which class?

examples.title: Competitive inhibition
examples.problem: Why does malonate inhibit succinic dehydrogenase?
examples.solution: Malonate closely resembles succinate, binds the active site and blocks it — competitive inhibition.

examples.title: Starch vs cellulose
examples.problem: Why does starch turn blue with iodine but cellulose doesn't?
examples.solution: Starch forms helical secondary structures that can hold I₂ molecules; cellulose has no such complex helices.

examples.title: Haemoglobin structure
examples.problem: What is the quaternary structure of adult haemoglobin?
examples.solution: Four subunits — two α and two β chains — each holding a haem group.

examples.title: Holoenzyme
examples.problem: An enzyme loses activity when its cofactor is removed. What does this show?
examples.solution: The protein part (apoenzyme) alone is inactive; the cofactor is essential, together forming the active holoenzyme.

topics.title: Primary and secondary metabolites
topics.explain: Primary metabolites (amino acids, sugars) have known roles in normal physiology. Secondary metabolites in plants, fungi and microbes include pigments (carotenoids, anthocyanins), alkaloids (morphine, codeine), terpenoids (monoterpenes, diterpenes), essential oils (lemongrass oil), toxins (abrin, ricin), lectins (concanavalin A), drugs (vinblastine, curcumin), polymeric substances (rubber, gums, cellulose).

topics.title: Metabolic basis for living
topics.explain: Metabolites are converted into each other by metabolic pathways — anabolic (biosynthetic, consume energy) and catabolic (degradation, release energy). ATP is the energy currency. The living state is a non-equilibrium steady state that can do work.

topics.title: Nature of enzyme action
topics.explain: Substrate binds the active site to form an enzyme–substrate complex (ES), the transition state forms, products are released and the enzyme is free to act again. Enzymes lower the activation energy; ribozymes are nucleic acids that act as enzymes.

topics.title: Proteins and their roles
topics.explain: Collagen (intercellular ground substance), trypsin (enzyme), insulin (hormone), antibodies (fight infection), receptors (sensory reception, e.g. smell), GLUT-4 (glucose transport into cells).

topics.title: Effect of substrate concentration
topics.explain: Velocity rises with substrate concentration and then reaches a maximum (Vmax) when all active sites are filled.

topics.title: Nucleic acid structure basics
topics.explain: In nucleic acids, the phosphate links the 3′ carbon of one sugar to the 5′ carbon of the next. B-DNA (Watson–Crick model) has 10 base pairs per turn, 3.4 nm pitch and 0.34 nm between base pairs.

ratta: Collagen — most abundant animal protein;  RuBisCO — biosphere.
Six classes: Oxido, Trans, Hydro, Lyase, Iso, Ligase.
Haem — prosthetic;  NAD (niacin) — coenzyme;  Zn²⁺ — carboxypeptidase.
Reductionist biology = physico-chemical approach to study and understand living organisms.
Transferase: S–G + S′ → S + S′–G;  lyase leaves a double bond;  ligase joins two molecules.
Adenosine = nucleoside;  adenylic acid = nucleotide;  adenine = base;  alanine = amino acid.
